questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the internal from the external sense of sovereignty
questions.stem: Sovereignty is described in two distinct senses, internal and external. Which concern belongs to each of them?

options.text: Internal: supremacy of the state at home; external: independence from other states
Internal: independence from other states; external: supremacy within the country
options.misconception: reverses which sense is about the domestic and which the external

options.text: Internal: the power to levy taxes; external: the power to wage war
options.misconception: reduces each sense to a single prerogative

options.text: Internal: recognition by other states; external: a seat in an international assembly
options.misconception: makes the external sense a matter of standing in one organisation

questions.explanation: The two senses ask different questions and are answered by different facts. The internal sense asks whether any authority within the state can lawfully set itself above another, which is a question about the domestic constitution and the reach of its courts. The external sense asks whether any other state can dictate to this one, which is a question about recognition, intervention and the legal equality of states. Each of the distractors either swaps the two or shrinks one of them to a single power, and the last answer in particular mistakes an external dimension for the whole of it, since a seat in one assembly is an instance of standing rather than the definition.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two questions is about other states and which is about one's own.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Why a state accepts a limit
questions.learningObjective: explain a state's reason for accepting a treaty limit
questions.stem: A state signs a treaty that limits the freedom of action its government would otherwise have. What explains that decision without assuming the government overlooked the limit?

options.text: The reciprocal restraint it gains against others, or the issues it cannot settle alone
That the treaty in fact leaves the state's freedom of action entirely unchanged
options.misconception: explains a real limit by denying that the limit exists

options.text: That no other state has signed a comparable treaty at the same time
options.misconception: invents a situation of solitary restraint

options.text: That its own constitution forbids it from acting on the subject alone
options.misconception: grounds an international choice in a rule of domestic constitutional law

questions.explanation: A limit is worth accepting when it buys something that could not be obtained by acting alone. A state that binds itself against a practice gains the same restraint from every other state that has bound itself, which is a gain no unilateral decision can deliver, and some problems cannot be handled by one actor however willing it is. That is the ordinary logic behind most commitments and it requires no oversight by the government. The remaining answers each remove the constraint rather than explain it: the first denies the limit, the second posits a situation the case does not describe, and the third imports a domestic rule to carry the weight of an international choice.
questions.hint: Ask what the state obtains in exchange for the restraint it accepts.

questions.learningObjective: identify the principal-agent problem in international bodies
questions.stem: A group of states transfers decisions to a body of officials, which creates a problem of principal and agent. What is that problem?

options.text: The officials know more than the states and may act to serve their own purposes
The states disagree among themselves about which outcome they want
options.misconception: describes a disagreement over preferences rather than a problem of delegation

options.text: The officials lack the legal authority to make binding decisions
options.misconception: denies the very authority that the delegation was made to supply

options.text: The states cannot meet often enough to give the officials instructions
options.misconception: reports a scheduling difficulty as though it were the central difficulty

questions.explanation: The problem arises from two features of the arrangement: the delegates know more about the subject than the states that appointed them, and once the decision is made the states cannot see everything the officials did or intend to do. Information of that kind gives the agent scope to pursue objectives the principals would not choose, which is the standard hazard wherever authority is handed to a body the principals do not control. The other options describe different problems: a preference disagreement is a problem among principals rather than between principal and agent, and a lack of authority would defeat the delegation rather than complicate it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify the effects a treaty extract establishes

stimulus.body: Treaty extract, written for this question. Article 2: each state party shall bring its national implementing rules into conformity with this treaty within two years of the date on which it enters into force for that state. Article 3: a state party that is not able to achieve conformity shall notify the depositary of that fact and of its reasons and shall report thereafter once a year. Article 4: any dispute concerning the interpretation of this treaty shall be settled by a commission of three members, one appointed by each of two disputing states and one by a third state they agree between them.

questions.stem: A treaty extract requires each state party to bring its national implementing rules into conformity within two years of entry into force for that state; requires a state unable to achieve conformity to notify the depositary with reasons and to report annually; and sends interpretation disputes to a commission of three members. Which observation does the extract support?

options.text: The treaty sets a standard, a reporting duty and a procedure, but attaches no penalty
Each state party may substitute a stricter rule of its own choosing
options.misconception: describes an option the conformity duty does not offer

options.text: The annual report creates a route to a state's removal from the treaty
options.misconception: reads a reporting obligation as though it were a sanction

options.text: The commission may compel a state to bring its rules into conformity
options.misconception: gives a settlement body an enforcement power it is not granted

questions.explanation: Each article does one job and the three together define the character of the arrangement. Article 2 states the standard, article 3 creates a reporting duty that makes non-conformity visible without punishing it, and article 4 supplies a procedure for interpretive disputes. What none of the three provides is a consequence: no article is described as expelling a state or compelling conformity, so the enforcement machinery in the extract is procedural and reporting rather than penal. That is why the correct answer is the one that lists what is there, and why the alternatives, each of which adds a mechanism the text omits, fail.
questions.hint: Check whether any article states a consequence for failing to conform.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: distinguish monist from dualist systems on treaty law
questions.stem: In one legal system a ratified treaty operates as domestic law without a further step; in another it must first be transformed into domestic law by the legislature. What is the difference between those systems?

options.text: Whether an international commitment needs a further domestic step before it operates at home
Whether the treaty binds other states as well as the state that ratified it
options.misconception: turns a question of domestic operation into one about external binding force

options.text: Whether judges or legislators have the better claim to interpret the text
options.misconception: reduces the distinction to a division of functions inside the state

options.text: Whether the state's courts may decline to apply a ratified commitment
options.misconception: asserts a supremacy question the distinction does not raise

questions.explanation: The distinction concerns how an international commitment enters a state's own law. Where the two systems are treated as one, ratification is enough for the commitment to operate before the domestic courts without any further act. Where they are separate, the commitment must be received into domestic law by the ordinary legislative process, and until that happens it binds the state internationally without being enforceable before its own courts. That is a structural difference about the route a rule takes, not about who interprets it, how broadly it binds or whether courts may resist it, which is what the other answers choose to argue about.
questions.hint: Ask what has to happen domestically before the commitment can be applied in a domestic court.

questions.learningObjective: compute the threshold and veto share in a 15-member council

Eight votes carry a matter, which is just over half, and the veto sits with a fifth
options.misconception: uses a bare majority of fifteen and understates the veto's share

options.text: Fifteen votes are required, since every member holds an equal veto
options.misconception: turns the veto held by five into a veto held by all

options.text: Ten votes carry a matter, which is two thirds, and the veto sits with a third
options.misconception: overstates the threshold while stating the veto's share correctly

questions.explanation: A simple majority of 15 is 8, but a bare majority has to clear the halfway point, and the figure that does so is 9, which is 60 percent of the council. Five of fifteen is a third, so a third of the members can block a matter outright, which is the reason the veto is treated as a structural feature rather than a detail. The remaining answers each contain one true element and one false one: eight is the arithmetic floor but not a majority, ten is two thirds rather than a majority, and fifteen would be unanimity, which is a different rule from the five vetoes the description states.
questions.hint: Clear the halfway point of fifteen, then divide the five veto holders by fifteen.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a signalling reason from an instrumental one
questions.stem: Two reasons are offered for a state's signature on a treaty: that the treaty will change what it actually does, or that the signature tells others something. What is the second reason called?

options.text: Signalling, in which the value of the act lies in what it reveals to others
Ratification, in which the act acquires domestic legal force
options.misconception: names a domestic procedure as though it were a reason for signing

options.text: Reciprocity, in which each state's act obliges the others
options.misconception: labels an exchange of obligations as a communicative act

options.text: Termination, in which a treaty ends by notice rather than by breach
options.misconception: describes how a treaty ends rather than why one is signed

questions.explanation: The two reasons answer different questions. An instrumental reason holds that the commitment will change behaviour, and it can be tested by looking at what the state does afterwards. A signalling reason holds that the commitment is valuable because it conveys a disposition, whether of resolve, of good faith or of alignment, and it can be tested by looking at how others adjust their behaviour in response. Ratification is a domestic step that may be required before obligations attach, reciprocity describes the exchange of commitments rather than the communicative effect, and termination concerns the end of a treaty rather than the reason for entering it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the value lies in what the treaty does or in what the act reveals.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: interpret a withdrawal clause
questions.stem: A treaty provides that a state may withdraw on twelve months' written notice. What does that clause authorise the withdrawing state to do?

options.text: To be released from the treaty's obligations once the notice period has run
To be released from its obligations on the day the notice is given
options.misconception: ignores the notice period the clause sets out

options.text: To be released from its obligations while keeping the benefits the treaty confers
options.misconception: separates duties from benefits in a way the clause does not

options.text: Nothing, because only a collective decision can bring a treaty to an end
options.misconception: denies the unilateral route the clause expressly provides

questions.explanation: A withdrawal clause specifies the conditions and the timing of a unilateral exit, and its whole effect depends on both. Here the condition is written notice and the timing is twelve months, so the obligations continue during that period and end when it expires. That is why the first answer is the accurate one and the second is not: the clause is about release after a period, not about immediate release on the day notice is served. A clause cannot detach the benefits from the burdens, since that is precisely what membership consists of, and the fourth answer denies the possibility the clause creates.
questions.hint: Ask what the notice starts and when the obligations actually end.

questions.learningObjective: select the costs of international organisation membership
questions.stem: What does membership of an international organisation normally cost a member state? Select all that apply.

options.text: A share of the budget, fixed by a formula the members themselves approve
Acceptance of the rules the organisation sets for conduct within its field
The capacity to act alone on subjects the organisation has taken over
A veto over every decision the organisation takes
options.misconception: assumes a general veto that few memberships grant

options.text: Legal immunity for the state's own officials within its own territory
options.misconception: carries an international privilege into domestic law

questions.explanation: Membership is a package of costs and the three listed are its ordinary components. A budget contribution is the price of the organisation's machinery, the rules on conduct bind the member within the field the organisation covers, and a subject that has been transferred to it can no longer be handled unilaterally, which is the autonomy the state gives up. The two remaining items are not typical costs: most memberships confer no veto over ordinary decisions, and immunity granted in an international setting says nothing about the reach of law inside the member's own territory. The price of joining is money, rules and shared authority, not either of the last two.
questions.hint: Ask what the state hands over, and whether the item describes something any membership confers.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify the monitoring problem in conditional finance
questions.stem: An international financier releases a loan only if the borrowing state adopts specified policies. What is the central difficulty the financier faces once the conditions are met?

options.text: It cannot observe the borrower's implementation after the money has been released
The borrower cannot refuse the offer without losing all of its other finance
options.misconception: invents a take-it-or-leave-it position the case does not describe

options.text: The required policies are chosen by the lender, so they reflect the lender's interests
options.misconception: assumes a motive where the difficulty described is one of information

options.text: The loan must be repaid in foreign currency, so the borrower may default
options.misconception: substitutes a debt-servicing risk for a problem about compliance

questions.explanation: Conditionality depends on verification, and verification is what becomes harder once the money moves. Before disbursement the financier can attach reports, audits and review missions to the funds, and the pressure of a pending payment keeps the borrower's attention on the conditions. Afterwards the same leverage is gone, the state has the money, and compliance is observable only to the extent that the state's own institutions report on it, so the gap between a formal condition and actual practice tends to widen. That is the information problem the arrangement creates, and it is why the other options, which describe a refusal option the case does not state, a motive and a currency risk, all describe something other than the difficulty in the case.
questions.hint: Ask what changes about the financier's leverage once the money has been paid.

questions.learningObjective: identify the concern raised by a fixed-term delegate
questions.stem: A state's delegate to a standing body serves a nine-year term and cannot be dismissed by the government that appointed her. What concern does that arrangement create?

options.text: The delegate's loyalty may outlast the government that appointed her
The delegate can no longer be instructed by her own government at all
options.misconception: reports a complete severing of instructions where only the term changes

options.text: The body can no longer remove a delegate who proves unhelpful
options.misconception: treats the fixed term as a protection the body enjoys

options.text: The state's votes are removed from the body's calculations
options.misconception: reports an exclusion of the state from the body's arithmetic

questions.explanation: The term protects the delegate and that is the point of it, since a delegate who could be dismissed the moment she was difficult would be an instruction-taker rather than a representative. The cost falls on the state, whose government can be replaced while the delegate continues to speak and to form relationships inside the body for years after the change. That is a real concern about the responsiveness of the body's membership, and the arrangement is often defended as a way of keeping delegates from being mere representatives of a current majority. What it does not do is sever instructions altogether, protect the body from removal, or remove the state's votes from anything.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two the fixed term serves, and what that leaves uncared for.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A binding instrument and a non-binding one
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a binding commitment from a statement of intent
questions.stem: A memorandum between governments records an intention and is described as not binding. How does such a document differ from a treaty?

options.text: It states a purpose without creating an obligation the parties can be held to
It binds only the states that signed it, unlike a treaty
options.misconception: reports a rule about which states are bound that treaties also observe

options.text: It lapses at the end of the year in which it was signed
options.misconception: invents a sunset rule the document need not contain

options.text: It is confidential, whereas treaties are published in full
options.misconception: confuses publication with legal force

questions.explanation: The distinction is one of legal character, and it turns on what the parties have undertaken. A binding instrument sets obligations whose breach is a wrong that generates a right of response, whether in kind, in compensation or in cessation, and a memorandum of intention creates none of that, which is why governments use one or the other deliberately. Confidentiality is a matter of disclosure and publication bears on the character of a text, not on whether it binds. Nor does a non-binding document have a rule about which states it reaches, since it binds nobody at all, and a lapsing date is something a document must state rather than something inherent in the form.
questions.hint: Ask what follows if one of the parties ignores what the document says.

questions.learningObjective: identify the accountability concern in an unelected body
questions.stem: A global body makes decisions that bind member states, and no government elects the officials who lead it. Which concern follows from that arrangement?

options.text: Accountability to the governed runs indirectly, since no elected official chooses the leadership
The body's decisions must be void in the domestic law of every member state
options.misconception: infers a defect in authority that invalidates the act at home

options.text: No state may take part unless it separately elects the leadership itself
options.misconception: invents a participation rule that would exclude every member

options.text: The body must be staffed by elected officials rather than by representatives
options.misconception: prescribes a composition the arrangement already has

questions.explanation: Democratic accountability normally runs through a chain of elections, and where the top of a body is not chosen by any electorate that chain is broken at the top. Member governments are answerable to their own citizens, but no citizen elects the officials who lead the body, so the connection between those affected and those deciding is indirect and mediated through the member states. That is the substance of the concern, and it is a real one whether or not the body's rulings are enforceable at home. The other answers each go beyond it: a defect in electoral connection does not by itself void a decision, and neither a participation bar nor a change of composition follows from the arrangement described.
questions.hint: Ask which officeholders no citizen has any electoral route to.

questions.topic: A two-thirds threshold in a large assembly
questions.learningObjective: compute a two-thirds threshold in a 193-member assembly
questions.stem: An assembly of 193 member states votes on a matter that its rules place in the two-thirds category. How many affirmative votes are required, and how much more than a bare majority is that?

97 votes, since a bare majority already reaches the two-thirds threshold
options.misconception: reports a bare majority as though it satisfied a two-thirds rule

options.misconception: truncates a fractional threshold instead of rounding to a whole vote

questions.hint: Two thirds of 193 is not a whole number, so round in the direction the rule requires.

questions.topic: Characteristics of a global public good
questions.learningObjective: identify the consequences of a non-excludable and non-rival good
questions.stem: A good counts as global when one state's use of it does not reduce what is left for others, and no state can be kept out of its benefits. What follows for the states that use it?

options.text: Each benefits from others' restraint, so it has an interest in their restraint as well
Each gains nothing from the good unless it alone pays the whole cost
options.misconception: makes access to the benefit depend on paying in full

options.text: One state's use always reduces what remains available to the others
options.misconception: states the opposite of the property that defines the good

options.text: Only the state that produces the good can be kept out of it
options.misconception: reverses which state may be excluded from the benefit

questions.explanation: The two defining properties together create the interest structure that makes such goods difficult to provide. Because use is non-rival, a state that abstains loses nothing that another state's contribution would have preserved, and because the good is non-excludable it cannot be kept out. The other answers each contradict one of the two properties, and the second in particular confuses a payment with an entitlement, since a good that cannot be excluded is not made unavailable by a refusal to pay.

questions.learningObjective: define free-riding and its threat to supply

questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages by which a commitment becomes binding
questions.stem: Put these five stages in the order a state typically passes through when a matter moves from a political proposal to an obligation it is legally bound by.

options.text: Negotiators settle the text of an instrument at a diplomatic conference
A state signs the instrument, recording its consent to be bound
The state completes whatever domestic approval its own law requires
The number of ratifications the instrument requires is reached and it enters into force
The state brings its own rules into line with the obligations it has accepted

questions.explanation: The order runs from drafting to domestic compliance, and each stage depends on the one before it. A text has to be settled by negotiators before any state can consent to it, and consent is recorded by signature rather than by anything the state does internally. The domestic approval comes next and is a matter of the state's own constitution, which is why it cannot be assumed from the signature. Entry into force is a collective event that depends on the required number of ratifications, so a state bound by the instrument is bound from a date it does not choose alone, and only after that date does implementation in its own law become the remaining task. So the sequence is A, B, C, D, E.
questions.hint: Ask which stage fixes a date no single state can decide.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Why states comply with rules they did not write
questions.learningObjective: explain why a state complies with a rule it did not make
questions.stem: Explain why a state complies with an international rule that other states wrote and it did not, and name one cost that compliance imposes on it.

answer.exemplar: There are three sources of such compliance, and they work through different mechanisms. The first is reciprocal. A state that has spent years in a negotiation has invested in a regime of rules it did not draft, and it is unlikely to be treated well by partners who have learned that it does not honour commitments, so the value of the whole system to it exceeds the value of any one breach. The second is legal and institutional. A rule may be incorporated into domestic law, and a state that breaches it then has to explain to its own courts and legislature why, which converts an external dispute into a domestic one that is far more costly. The third is the reduction of uncertainty. States that have signed tend to adjust their own policies to what the rules permit and in some cases build on them, and a breach requires dismantling arrangements already in place rather than simply declining to build new ones. The costs follow from the same structure. Compliance is not free: a state constrained by a rule on emissions, on taxation or on procurement may find a policy it wanted ruled out, and it may be pressed by domestic producers to protect their position. It also forgoes the option of waiting to see whether others will comply first, which is the option a self-interested state would most like to keep. So the reasons that produce compliance are the same features that make it costly.

questions.explanation: A model answer should identify at least two sources of compliance, such as reciprocity, domestic legal incorporation, or the cost of unwinding existing arrangements, and should name a cost such as a foreclosed policy option or domestic pressure from affected interests.
questions.hint: Ask what the state has already invested in the rule, and what it would have to dismantle to break it.

questions.learningObjective: evaluate the claim that a treaty abolishes sovereignty
questions.stem: A government argues that ratifying a treaty surrenders its sovereignty over the subject the treaty covers. Which consideration most seriously weakens that claim?

options.text: Consent to a limit is itself a sovereign act rather than the giving up of sovereignty
The text was drafted by other states, so consent to it cannot be genuine
options.misconception: treats the authorship of a text as though it voided consent to it

options.text: Sovereignty has no meaning at all for a state that has signed any treaty
options.misconception: generalises a claim about one subject to the whole of the state's position

options.text: The state may always denounce the treaty and recover its complete freedom
options.misconception: assumes withdrawal restores the position before any commitment was made

questions.explanation: Sovereignty is a capacity to decide, and a state that binds itself has exercised that capacity rather than exhausted it. The claim also overstates the extent of what has been given up: a treaty limits action in the area it covers and leaves the rest untouched, and the state retains the institutions, the consent and the withdrawal provisions that make the arrangement what it is. The other answers either deny that consent can be genuine because others drafted the text, generalise from one subject to all, or assume that denouncing a treaty restores a position that was never there.
questions.hint: Ask whether a state can be bound without having decided to be bound.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Whether a compliance history is credible
questions.learningObjective: explain why compliance history bears on reliance
questions.stem: Explain why a state's record of honouring undertakings matters to other states deciding whether to rely on the one it has just given, and name one reason a state might break a rule it accepted.

answer.exemplar: Reliance is a decision taken under uncertainty, and the record is the only evidence available. A state considering whether to reduce its own preparations, or to disclose a plan, or to hand over control of a mechanism, cannot observe compliance in advance, so it estimates the probability from conduct. A state with a long record of performance is offering evidence rather than a promise, and that evidence is what allows the other party to accept an irreversible step. A state whose record includes breaches forces the other side either to forgo the benefit or to protect itself with costly safeguards, and in a setting where relationships are repeated the reputational cost of that caution is itself a penalty. Breaches do occur for identifiable reasons. Domestic politics may make a measure that was easy to promise very hard to maintain once a change of government or of leadership occurs, and a state that has to choose between an unpopular commitment and a domestic crisis will often take the crisis. A government may also reassess the costs of a commitment made under different conditions, or conclude that the benefit it expected has not materialised. Or the breach may follow from a change in the facts the rule was written to address, in which case the state believes the obligation has been overtaken rather than that it has been broken. What all these have in common is that they are reasons visible to others, which is why an explanation offered after the fact affects the credibility of the next undertaking as well.

questions.explanation: A model answer should explain that reliance requires estimating future conduct from past conduct, and should name a reason such as a domestic political reversal, a reassessment of costs, or a change in the underlying facts.

States invest on the assumption that they know what a commitment requires, so a construction that extends a rule into new ground removes the basis for that investment and gives those who administer it a discretion to exercise at other people's expense. The other answers confuse this with unrelated matters. Consent is not withdrawn by interpretation, difficulty in reaching an interpretation says nothing about what it requires once reached, and criticism of the drafters' wording is a comment on the text rather than on the state that has to comply with it.
questions.hint: Ask what a state cannot do if it does not know how far a rule reaches.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Payment rates and a voting threshold
questions.learningObjective: apply a payment threshold to identify which state loses a vote
questions.stem: First stage: an organisation requires members to pay at least 80 percent of their assessed contribution to keep their vote in a subsidiary body. Five members are assessed 30, 20, 15, 10 and 5 units, and have paid 24, 16, 12, 4 and 5 units. Second stage: which member loses its vote, and what does the overall payment rate come to?

options.text: The member assessed 10 and paid 4, at 40 percent, and the overall rate is about 76 percent
The member assessed 30 and paid 24, at 80 percent, and the overall rate is about 76 percent
options.misconception: names a state that meets the threshold exactly as the one that fails

options.text: The member assessed 20 and paid 16, at 80 percent, and the overall rate is 100 percent
options.misconception: names a compliant state and reports a rate the payments do not produce

options.text: No member loses its vote, since every payment is close to the assessment
options.misconception: reads the payments as uniformly near the assessed amounts they are not near

questions.explanation: The rule is a threshold, so the comparison is each member's payment with its own assessment, not with the average. Twenty-four of thirty, sixteen of twenty and twelve of fifteen are all exactly 80 percent and all satisfy a rule that requires at least 80; five of five is 100 percent and satisfies it too. Four of ten is 40 percent and fails, so that member loses its vote, and the reason it is the fourth in the list is that it is the only one far below its assessment. Across all five the assessment is 80 units and the payments total 61, so the overall rate is 61 out of 80, or about 76 percent, below the rate the rule applies to individuals.
questions.hint: Divide each payment by that member's own assessment, not by the total.

questions.topic: A funding split between two contributors
questions.learningObjective: assess a funding split from a stated total

stimulus.body: Funding note, written for this question. A programme with a total budget of 2,400 million is funded by two parties. The first contributes 720 million, agreed as a fixed share set for the whole period. The second contributes 1,680 million, and the note records that its contribution was calculated as the balance required after the first party's share had been deducted. The note also states that the second party's share is more than twice the first party's.

questions.stem: A programme with a total budget of 2,400 million is funded by two parties. The first contributes 720 million, fixed in advance for the whole period; the second contributes 1,680 million, calculated as the balance after the first party's share was deducted; and the note records that the second share is more than twice the first. What does the note establish about the split?

options.text: A 30 to 70 split, in which the larger contributor is funded as the residual share
An even split, since a two-party programme divides its budget equally
options.misconception: assumes parity where the stated figures are unequal

options.text: A 70 to 30 split, with the residual share falling on the first party
options.misconception: reverses which contributor bears the balance

options.text: A split that exceeds what the first party had agreed to by some margin
options.misconception: invents an over-run where the note records agreement to a fixed share

questions.explanation: The two contributions and the total are consistent with a straightforward calculation. The first party's 720 out of 2,400 is 30 percent, the second party's 1,680 is 70 percent, the two add back to the stated total, and 1,680 is more than twice 720, which is the relationship the note records. The second statement also identifies what makes the arrangement a bargaining feature rather than a neutral one: a residual share is whatever the other parties fail to provide, so the party whose contribution is computed last carries the risk of a shortfall and will press hardest for the fixed share to be set low. The other answers each contradict the figures or import an obligation the note does not record.
questions.hint: Divide each contribution by the total, and check that the two shares add to 100 percent.
